questions.q: What is the inferred return type of async function countOrders() { return 42; }?
questions.explain: An async function always returns a promise. Its value type comes from the return statements, widened like any inferred return type, so it is Promise<number>.

questions.q: Why does async function getBalance(): number { return 250000; } fail to compile?
questions.explain: Error TS1064: the function returns a promise whatever its body does, so the annotation must say Promise<number>. The body still returns the plain number.
options: Because an async function's return type must be Promise<T>; the annotation should be Promise<number>
Because async functions cannot have a return type annotation
Because return is not allowed in async functions

questions.q: Inside async function getRate(): Promise<number> { … }, which return statement does not compile?
questions.explain: The return expression is checked against the awaited type, number. A number or a promise of a number are both fine, because promises flatten. A string is not a number.

questions.q: What is the type of const rate = new Promise((resolve) => resolve(1540.25));?
questions.explain: The constructor's T is not inferred from what you pass to resolve. Without a type argument or a contextual type (such as a function's return type), it is unknown. Write new Promise<number>(…).

questions.q: What is Awaited<Promise<Promise<string>> | number>?
questions.explain: Awaited unwraps promises recursively, like await does, and leaves non-promise types alone. It applies to each member of a union.

questions.q: A helper is async function logged<T>(task: () => T) { return await task(); }. Which return type is honest?
questions.explain: If task returns a promise, T is that promise, but await unwraps it. Promise<T> would claim the helper resolves to a promise. Promise<Awaited<T>> describes what really happens for both sync and async tasks.

questions.q: loadUser() returns Promise<User> and countOrders() returns Promise<number>. What does await Promise.all([loadUser(), countOrders()]) give?
questions.explain: With an array literal, Promise.all keeps the positions: a tuple with the awaited type of each input. await removes the outer promise.

questions.q: Now the promises are stored first: const jobs = [loadUser(), countOrders()]; const results = await Promise.all(jobs);. What is the type of results?
questions.explain: jobs is inferred as an array of a union, (Promise<User> | Promise<number>)[], so the positions are gone. as const on jobs, or passing the literal directly, keeps the tuple.

questions.q: What is the type of await Promise.all(accountIds.map((id) => loadAccount(id))), where loadAccount returns Promise<Account>?
questions.explain: map produces Promise<Account>[], an array of one kind of promise, and Promise.all turns it into Account[]. An array type is exactly right when every element has the same type.

questions.q: What is the type of await Promise.race([loadName(), countOrders()]), where they return Promise<string> and Promise<number>?
questions.explain: race settles with whichever input settles first, so the result may come from either: the union of the awaited types.

questions.q: A timeout helper creates new Promise<never>((_, reject) => …) and races it against a Promise<T>. Why never?
questions.explain: never is the type with no values: exactly what a promise that only rejects produces. It disappears from unions, so Promise.race([task, timeout]) keeps the type Promise<T>.
options: Because a timeout promise must not be awaited
Because it can only reject, never produce a value, and T | never is just T, so callers get their own type back

questions.q: In a PromiseRejectedResult from Promise.allSettled, what is the type of reason?
questions.explain: Rejections have no type in TypeScript, and the library types this property as any. Treat it as unknown and narrow it, the same rule as for catch variables.
options: any, so it is worth copying into an unknown variable before using it

questions.q: const [rate] = await Promise.allSettled([loadRate()]); How do you safely read the rate?
questions.explain: PromiseSettledResult<T> is a union discriminated by status. Only the fulfilled member has value, so the compiler requires the check.

questions.q: Why does orders.filter(async (order) => await isPaid(order)) keep every order?
questions.explain: filter is synchronous and tests the callback's return value right away. A pending promise is an object, and objects are truthy. The compiler accepts it because filter's callback may return unknown.
options: Because the callback returns a promise, and every promise object is truthy
Because filter waits for the promises but ignores false
Because async functions cannot be passed to array methods

questions.q: A function runs orderIds.forEach(async (id) => { await sendReceipt(id); }) and then logs "done". When is "done" logged?
questions.explain: forEach starts each callback, ignores the promise it returns, and returns immediately. Use for...of with await, or await Promise.all(orderIds.map(sendReceipt)).
options: After the first receipt is sent
Before any receipt has finished sending

questions.q: Which typescript-eslint rule reports an async function passed where a callback's return value is ignored, as in forEach(async …)?
questions.explain: no-misused-promises catches promises in places that expect void or a boolean-ish value; its sibling no-floating-promises catches promises that nobody handles. The compiler cannot see either.

questions.q: What does the return type AsyncGenerator<Transaction, number, undefined> say about an async function*?
questions.explain: The three parameters are the yield type, the return type (seen as value when done is true) and the type next(value) accepts.
options: It yields numbers and returns transactions
It yields Transaction values, returns a number when it finishes, and expects nothing from next()
It returns an array of transactions and a count
It accepts a Transaction through next() and yields numbers

questions.q: What must an object have so that for await (const item of object) compiles against AsyncIterable<T>?
questions.explain: The async iteration protocol starts at Symbol.asyncIterator. An async *[Symbol.asyncIterator]() generator method is the shortest way to provide it, and implements AsyncIterable<T> lets the compiler check it.
options: A [Symbol.asyncIterator]() method that returns an async iterator

questions.q: A pager is an async generator that fetches the next page only when the previous page's items are used up. A loop over it hits break on page 2 of 10. How many pages were fetched?
questions.explain: A generator only runs when the loop asks for the next value, and break finishes it. So only the pages needed to reach the break are requested.
options: 3, because it fetches one page ahead

questions.q: What is the type of await response.json() with TypeScript's DOM types, and what should you do about it?
questions.explain: The DOM's json() returns Promise<any>, which silently switches off checking for everything downstream. const data: unknown = await response.json() closes the hole, and a parser turns it into a checked type. (In a Node-only project, with "lib": ["ES2024"] and @types/node, json() is already typed Promise<unknown>; the annotation costs nothing and keeps the code safe under either.)
options: any; annotate the result as unknown and parse it with a checking function
object; cast it to your interface with as
The type of the interface you pass as a type argument

questions.q: Why does the timeout helper declare let timer: ReturnType<typeof setTimeout> | undefined?
questions.explain: Deriving the type from the function avoids hard-coding either environment's timer type. The | undefined is because it is assigned inside the promise executor.
options: Because setTimeout returns a Timeout object in Node and a number in browsers, and this type follows whichever environment you compile for

questions.q: What does Promise.withResolvers<PaymentEvent>() give you?
questions.explain: It is new Promise with the two functions handed back to you, typed by the same T. It suits results that arrive later from somewhere else, such as a webhook.
options: { promise, resolve, reject }, where promise is Promise<PaymentEvent> and resolve only accepts a PaymentEvent
A function that converts callbacks into promises

questions.q: Write delay(ms: number): Promise<void> with new Promise and setTimeout, and after<T>(ms: number, value: T): Promise<T> that resolves with value after ms milliseconds.
questions.explain: The return type gives new Promise its T by contextual typing, so resolve accepts exactly T (or nothing, for void). The shorter delay finishes first.

questions.q: Finish withTimeout<T>: race task against a Promise<never> that rejects with Error(`${label} timed out`) after ms, and clear the timer in finally.
questions.explain: Promise<never> keeps the race's type Promise<T>. return await keeps the rejection inside the try, and finally clears the timer whichever side wins.

questions.q: This code loads a count and a product in parallel, but orders and product both have the union type number | { name: string }, so orders.toFixed(0) and product.name would not compile. Fix the types so each value keeps its own type (no as on the results), then print 42 orders; best seller: Ankara tote bag using orders.toFixed(0) and product.name.
questions.explain: as const keeps work as a readonly tuple, so Promise.all returns [number, { name: string }] and each variable has its own type. Passing the array literal straight to Promise.all works too.
questions.expected: 42 orders; best seller: Ankara tote bag

questions.q: Use Promise.allSettled to send all receipts, then print the successful values joined with " | ", and the number of failures.
questions.explain: The arrow functions that check status are inferred as type guards (TypeScript 5.5 and later), so after the first filter, .value is typed string with no cast.

questions.q: Write filterAsync<T>(items: readonly T[], predicate: (item: T) => Promise<boolean>): Promise<T[]> that runs all checks in parallel and keeps the items whose check resolved to true.
questions.explain: Get every boolean first with Promise.all and map, whose callback return type is kept, then filter synchronously. The starter's filter kept everything, because a promise is truthy.

questions.q: Finish the async generator paginate: fetch the page for the current cursor (start with null), yield each item, then move to nextCursor until it is null.
questions.explain: T is inferred from the fetch function, so id is a string. yield* hands out a page's items one by one, and the caller never sees pages or cursors. A production pager also limits the number of pages.

questions.q: Write collect<T>(source: AsyncIterable<T>, limit: number): Promise<T[]> that gathers at most limit items and then stops reading.
questions.explain: Accepting AsyncIterable<T> makes the helper work with any async source. Breaking as soon as the limit is reached stops the generator, so it never produces the fourth item.

questions.q: Wrap the callback API legacyGetRate in getRate(currency: string): Promise<number>. Reject with the error when there is one, and with new Error("no rate") when the rate is missing.
questions.explain: The return type Promise<number> types resolve, so the optional rate must be checked before it can be resolved. That check is also the runtime guard against an SDK that reports neither an error nor a value.
questions.expected:
USD 1540.25
XYZ unknown currency XYZ
GHS no rate
